title: Destructors
relevance: Interviewers use destructors to probe whether candidates understand deterministic cleanup, RAII, and the virtual-destructor rule that prevents leaks under polymorphic delete.

phases.goal: Establish what a destructor is, its syntax constraints, and when the compiler invokes it.

must_hit.point: A destructor is a special member function that runs automatically when an object is destroyed; its primary job is cleanup of resources acquired during the object's lifetime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says it auto-runs on destruction and exists to release owned resources, not to create the object.

must_hit.point: Destructor syntax is the class name preceded by a tilde; it takes no parameters (so cannot be overloaded), has no return type (not even void), and a class has exactly one destructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names ~ClassName and lists the three rules: no args, no return type, exactly one.

must_hit.point: Destructors are invoked automatically when a stack-allocated object goes out of scope or when a heap-allocated object is destroyed with delete.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names both scope-exit for locals and delete for heap objects as the two main trigger cases.

probes: What is a destructor, and when does the compiler call it?

hints.1: Think about what runs when an object's lifetime ends.
hints.2: Cover the ~Name syntax rules and the two invocation scenarios: leaving scope versus delete.
hints.3: A destructor is ~ClassName with no parameters and no return type; it runs on scope exit for stack objects and on delete for heap objects to perform cleanup.

phases.goal: Explain destruction order, when an explicit destructor is required, and how delete interacts with cleanup.

must_hit.point: When multiple local objects go out of scope, they are destroyed in the reverse order of construction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states last-constructed is first-destroyed for locals leaving the same scope.

must_hit.point: An explicit destructor is needed when the object owns a resource that will not clean itself up, such as heap memory, an open file handle, or a network socket; for classes with only basic types the compiler-generated destructor is enough.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts POD/basic-type classes with ownership of heap, files, or sockets requiring user-written cleanup.

must_hit.point: delete on a pointer first calls the object's destructor to release internal resources, then frees the memory for the object itself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sequences destructor body before reclaiming the object's own storage, as in the Player inventory example.

must_hit.point: Unlike Python's garbage-collected cleanup at an unpredictable time (where __del__ is rarely used), C++ destruction is deterministic: the destructor fires when the object goes out of scope or is deleted.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts deterministic C++ destructor timing with Python GC / __del__ unpredictability.

probes: If several local objects leave scope together, in what order are their destructors run, and when must you write one yourself?

hints.1: Consider construction order and whether the class owns something raw.
hints.2: Locals destroy opposite to construction; write a destructor only for owned non-self-cleaning resources; recall what delete does first.
hints.3: Destroy reverse of construction; write ~T when owning heap/file/socket; delete calls the destructor then frees the object; C++ timing is deterministic unlike Python GC.

phases.goal: Connect custom destructors to the Rule of Zero/Three/Five and to virtual versus non-virtual base destructors under polymorphism.

must_hit.point: Writing a custom destructor strongly implies the class manually manages a resource, so the compiler-generated copy constructor and copy assignment will almost certainly be wrong (shallow copies leading to double-free); the Rule of Three says if you need a user-defined destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment, you almost certainly need all three.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate links custom destructor to resource ownership and states Rule of Three for destructor/copy ctor/copy assign.

must_hit.point: Modern C++ expands this to the Rule of Five (also move constructor and move assignment) and prefers the Rule of Zero: use smart pointers and standard containers so you need not write any of those special members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names Rule of Five for moves and Rule of Zero as preferring library types over hand-rolled special members.

must_hit.point: If a base pointer owns a derived object and ~Base is not virtual, delete through the base pointer only runs ~Base, skipping the derived destructor; marking the base destructor virtual makes delete use dynamic dispatch so ~Derived runs first, then ~Base.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains non-virtual base dtor skips derived cleanup and that virtual ~Base fixes the call order via dynamic dispatch.

probes: If you write a destructor for a resource-owning class, what else should you consider, and why must a polymorphic base destructor be virtual?

hints.1: Think about copying that class and about deleting a derived object through a base pointer.
hints.2: Rule of Three/Five versus Rule of Zero; non-virtual ~Base versus virtual ~Base under delete via Base*.
hints.3: Custom dtor implies Rule of Three (and Five with moves) or prefer Rule of Zero; without virtual ~Base, delete via Base* skips ~Derived and can leak or cause undefined behaviour.

phases.goal: Apply RAII and the virtual-destructor rule to safe resource and hierarchy designs.

must_hit.point: RAII binds resource acquisition to constructors and release to destructors so that stack unwinding on exceptions or early returns still runs local destructors and reclaims resources deterministically.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes acquire-in-ctor / release-in-dtor and that scope exit or exceptions still clean up via stack unwinding.

must_hit.point: Practical RAII: tie a manual resource (open file or heap allocation) to a local stack object's lifetime so when that object dies its destructor cleans up the resource, as in FileLogger opening in the constructor and closing in the destructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks an example like FileLogger: open on construct, close in destructor, safe even if processData throws or returns early.

must_hit.point: For inheritance with polymorphic delete, the base class destructor must be virtual so deleting a derived object via a base pointer invokes the derived destructor and avoids memory leaks and undefined behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gives the interview answer: virtual base destructor ensures derived cleanup when deleted through Base*.

probes: How does RAII prevent resource leaks when an exception is thrown, and why must a base class destructor be virtual?

hints.1: Connect object lifetime on the stack to when cleanup code runs.
hints.2: Acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor; then consider Base* deleting a Derived.
hints.3: RAII: local object's destructor runs on unwind/scope exit and closes/frees the resource; virtual ~Base so delete via Base* runs ~Derived then ~Base.

tradeoffs.topic: Rule of Zero vs Rule of Three/Five
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A user-defined destructor signals manual resource ownership, so you almost certainly also need matching copy (Rule of Three) and, in modern C++, move operations (Rule of Five); prefer Rule of Zero by owning resources via smart pointers and standard containers so none of those special members are written by hand.

With polymorphism, a non-virtual base destructor means delete through Base* only runs ~Base and skips ~Derived (undefined behaviour / leaks); a virtual base destructor uses dynamic dispatch so ~Derived runs first, then ~Base.

For classes holding only basic types, the automatically generated destructor is enough because object memory is reclaimed automatically; write an explicit destructor when the object owns a resource that will not clean itself up (heap memory, file handle, network socket).

gotchas.trap: Deleting a Derived object through a Base* when ~Base is not virtual
gotchas.correction: Only ~Base runs; ~Derived is skipped, so owned resources like a derived heap array leak and the behavior is undefined — mark the base destructor virtual so dynamic dispatch calls ~Derived then ~Base.

gotchas.trap: Writing a custom destructor but leaving compiler-generated copy operations
gotchas.correction: Those copies are typically shallow for owned resources and can cause double-free; follow the Rule of Three (and Rule of Five with moves) or avoid custom special members via the Rule of Zero.

gotchas.trap: Relying on Python-style thinking that cleanup happens sometime later via a garbage collector
gotchas.correction: In C++ destruction is deterministic: the destructor runs when the object leaves scope or is deleted, which is what makes RAII exception-safe.
